intro: Lytham, on the Fylde coast of Lancashire, has a veteran sweet chestnut that a reader found and photographed for us. Its pale, barkless central stem has died back, and the living tree carries on in a ring of younger limbs around it, over a swollen, burred base. The reader puts it at 300 to 400 years old and about seven metres round, both their estimates. It stands on grass beside a surfaced path, north of the South Park estate.

trees.story:
At the heart of this sweet chestnut stands a pale, dead stem, bleached and stripped of bark, while the living tree carries on around it in a ring of younger limbs. That is how old chestnuts age. The original trunk dies back and the tree keeps going from its edges.

A reader found it in Lytham and sent us its photograph from the spot. They put it at 300 to 400 years old and about seven metres round the trunk, both by a reader's estimate. No register we checked lists it, so those numbers are theirs until somebody brings a tape and a record. Seven metres would make it a big chestnut by any measure, and the swollen, burred base in the photograph does not argue with them.

It stands on mown grass beside a surfaced path, in a wide canopy of fresh green leaves, with woodland behind. Sweet chestnut was planted across English estates from the Tudors onward, and Lytham was one, but nothing we have read says who planted this one or when.

If you know its history, or the ground it stands on, tell us.

question_meta: The veteran sweet chestnut of Lytham, Lancashire: 300 to 400 years old by a reader's estimate. Where it stands and what to look for.
question_answer: Lytham's oldest known tree on our map is a veteran sweet chestnut (Castanea sativa) beside a surfaced path north of the South Park estate. A reader who photographed it puts it at 300 to 400 years old and about seven metres round the trunk, both by their estimate.
question_context: No register we checked lists this chestnut, so its age and girth come from the reader who found it and sent its photograph with a GPS fix. The photograph shows the shape of an old sweet chestnut: the original central stem has died and lost its bark, standing pale in the middle, while a ring of younger living limbs carries a full green crown around it. Sweet chestnuts often age this way, dying back at the centre and living on at the edges, and a girth of seven metres would put it among the large ones. Who owns the ground is not confirmed; it can be seen from the path beside it. Sweet chestnut is not native to Britain; it was planted on estates and in parks for centuries, and the oldest in the country are counted among its largest trees. Nothing we have read says who planted this one or when. A tape round the trunk, or a record from the estate, would settle both numbers.

faq.q: How old is the Lytham sweet chestnut?
faq.a: 300 to 400 years by the estimate of the reader who found it. No register we checked gives an age.
About seven metres round the trunk by the reader's estimate; nobody has published a tape measurement.

faq.q: Why is the middle of the tree dead?
faq.a: Old sweet chestnuts often lose their central stem and keep living from a ring of younger limbs around it, which is what this one has done.
On grass beside a surfaced path north of the South Park estate in Lytham, at the point on the map where the reader photographed it.
